items.title: Pauli matrices and the two-qubit exchange operator
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement:
Use the usual complex field $\mathbb C$; its scalar metric is $d_{\mathbb C}(z,w)=|z-w|$ from [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. On $\mathbb C^2$, use the standard basis $e_0=(1,0)$, $e_1=(0,1)$ and inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=x_0\overline{y_0}+x_1\overline{y_1}$, linear in its first variable. On $\mathbb R^3$, define $a\cdot b:=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z$, $|a|:=\sqrt{a\cdot a}$ using the unique nonnegative square root from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and the standard unit vectors $\mathbf e_x=(1,0,0)$, $\mathbf e_y=(0,1,0)$, and $\mathbf e_z=(0,0,1)$.

Use the ordered tensor-product basis $(e_0\otimes e_0,e_0\otimes e_1,e_1\otimes e_0,e_1\otimes e_1)$ of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$. Its inner product is the linear-first product inner product, specified on elementary tensors by $\langle u\otimes v,u'\otimes v'\rangle=\langle u,u'\rangle\langle v,v'\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly. For two $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$, their tensor product acts by $(A\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv$ and is extended linearly.

Write $I_2:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for the identity on $\mathbb C^2$, use $I:=I_2$ when its domain is clear, and set $I_4:=I_2\otimes I_2$. Define the everywhere-defined matrices

$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Define the dimensionless exchange matrix

$$C:=\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x+\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y+\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z.$$

For a finite matrix $A$, $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ denotes the sum of its diagonal entries in the displayed basis. Each $\sigma_j$ and $C$ is Hermitian and has full finite-dimensional domain.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §§2.2–2.3
Damian Markham et al., Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.title: Finite two-qubit density matrices and separability
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement: Use the single-qubit space and ordered two-qubit basis from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]]. A one-qubit density matrix is a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix $\rho$ such that $\langle \rho x,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb C^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$. A two-qubit density matrix is defined in the same way on $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$, using the four-dimensional trace. A product density matrix is $\rho_A\otimes\rho_B$ for one-qubit density matrices $\rho_A,\rho_B$. A two-qubit density matrix is **separable** if it is a finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^m t_j\rho_{A,j}\otimes\rho_{B,j}$, where $t_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j=1}^m t_j=1$. A two-qubit density matrix that is not separable is **entangled**. This finite-convex-combination convention is the one used by the local threshold proof.

references.title: John Watrous, The Theory of Quantum Information, Chapter 2, §§2.1.2–2.1.3
Damian Markham et al., Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.title: Spectrum of the two-qubit Pauli exchange matrix
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement: For $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], the singlet vector $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplet vectors $e_0\otimes e_0$, $(e_0\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$, and $e_1\otimes e_1$ have eigenvalue $1$. Here $\sqrt2$ is the unique positive square root supplied by [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]. These four vectors are an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §2.3
Damian Markham et al., Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.strategy:
1.1 Applying the three tensor products in [F1] to the ordered basis $(00,01,10,11)$ gives the matrix with outer diagonal entries $1,1$, middle block $\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, and all other entries zero. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The outer basis vectors are eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$. The middle block sends $(01-10)/\sqrt2$ to $-3(01-10)/\sqrt2$ and $(01+10)/\sqrt2$ to $(01+10)/\sqrt2$. Since $(\sqrt2)^2=2$, each displayed middle vector has squared norm $(1+1)/2=1$; their inner product is $(1-1)/2=0$. They are also orthogonal to $00,11$, so together the four eigenvectors are an orthonormal basis and give the full spectrum. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Bloch-ball representation of a qubit density matrix
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement:
For every one-qubit density matrix $\rho$ in [[def-qsm-finite-two-qubit-state-and-separability]], there is a unique vector $a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)\in\mathbb R^3$ such that

$$\rho=\frac12(I+a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z).$$

The matrix is positive exactly when $|a|\le1$, where $|a|=\sqrt{a\cdot a}$ is the Euclidean norm defined in [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]]. The coordinates are $a_j=\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)$.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §2.2
John Watrous, The Theory of Quantum Information, Chapter 2, §§2.1.2–2.1.3

items.strategy:
1.1 Write $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}u&z\\\overline z&1-u\end{pmatrix}$, where $u\in\mathbb R$ because $\rho$ is Hermitian and the lower diagonal entry is fixed by $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Set $a_x=2\operatorname{Re}z$, $a_y=-2\operatorname{Im}z$, and $a_z=2u-1$. Direct substitution of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\rho=\tfrac12(I+a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z)$. Direct multiplication gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)=a_j$ for each $j$, so the entries of $\rho$ force uniqueness and each coefficient is real. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The displayed matrix $A:=a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a_z&a_x-ia_y\\a_x+ia_y&-a_z\end{pmatrix}$. Expanding its $2\times2$ determinant gives $\det(\lambda I-A)=\lambda^2-a_x^2-a_y^2-a_z^2=\lambda^2-|a|^2$. Thus the eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix $A$ are $|a|$ and $-|a|$, and those of $\rho=(I+A)/2$ are $(1+|a|)/2$ and $(1-|a|)/2$. By the density definition [F2], $\rho$ is positive semidefinite exactly when both are nonnegative, which is equivalent to $|a|\le1$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Pauli exchange expectation bound for separable states
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement:
For every separable two-qubit density matrix $\rho$ and exchange operator $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]],
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho C)\ge-1.$$

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §2.3
Damian Markham et al., Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.strategy:
1.1 For qubit density matrices $\rho_A,\rho_B$ with Bloch vectors $a,b$, factorization of the finite matrix trace gives $\operatorname{tr}((\rho_A\otimes\rho_B)C)=\sum_{j=x,y,z}\operatorname{tr}(\rho_A\sigma_j)\operatorname{tr}(\rho_B\sigma_j)=a\cdot b$. By [F4] and [F2], $a\cdot b\ge-|a||b|\ge-1$. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Write a separable $\rho$ as $\sum_{k=1}^m p_k\rho^A_k\otimes\rho^B_k$ as in [F3]. Linearity of the trace and step 1.1 give $\operatorname{tr}(\rho C)=\sum_kp_k\operatorname{tr}((\rho^A_k\otimes\rho^B_k)C)\ge\sum_kp_k(-1)=-1$. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Explicit separable state at the Pauli dimer boundary
items.reference: Batch 46 local prerequisite support; placement rationale in research/physics-remaining-80-2026-10-17-batch-46.notes.md
items.design_state: Necessary mathematical prerequisite added to the assigned A page; included as inventory expansion in batch 46 evidence.
items.statement:
For $n\in\{\pm\mathbf e_x,\pm\mathbf e_y,\pm\mathbf e_z\}$, with the standard vectors from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], put $\rho_n=(I+n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z)/2$. The matrix
$$\rho_*:=\frac16\sum_{n\in\{\pm e_x,\pm e_y,\pm e_z\}}\rho_n\otimes\rho_{-n} =\frac14\left(I_4-\frac13C\right)$$
is a separable two-qubit density matrix.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §2.3
Damian Markham et al., Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.strategy:
1.1 Each vector $n$ in the six-term sum has exactly one coordinate equal to $1$ or $-1$ and the others zero, so the Euclidean norm in [F1] gives $|n|=1$. Thus [F3] makes $\rho_n$ and $\rho_{-n}$ qubit density matrices. The six terms have nonnegative equal weights $1/6$ summing to one; [F2] therefore proves that $\rho_*$ is separable. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For a fixed axis $\mathbf e_j$, direct expansion gives $\rho_{e_j}\otimes\rho_{-e_j}+\rho_{-e_j}\otimes\rho_{e_j}=\tfrac12(I_4-\sigma_j\otimes\sigma_j)$. Summing this identity over $j=x,y,z$ and dividing by six yields $\rho_*=\tfrac14I_4-\tfrac1{12}C=\tfrac14(I_4-C/3)$, as claimed. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite Pauli dimer spectrum and exact separability threshold
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement:
Use $C$ from [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], with singlet projection $P_s=|s\rangle\langle s|$ and triplet projection $P_t=I_4-P_s$, where $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$. For each dimensionless $x\ge0$, define the finite two-qubit density matrix
$$\rho_x:=\frac{e^{3x}P_s+e^{-x}P_t}{e^{3x}+3e^{-x}}.$$
Then $\rho_x$ is separable exactly when $x\le(\log 3)/4$, and it is entangled exactly when $x>(\log 3)/4$. In particular, the equality state at $x=(\log 3)/4$ is separable.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §2.3
Damian Markham, Janet Anders, Vlatko Vedral, Mio Murao, and Akimasa Miyake, Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.strategy:
1.1 The projections $P_s,P_t$ are orthogonal and have ranks one and three by [F1]. Their weighted sum in the definition of $\rho_x$ is therefore positive, and its trace is $e^{3x}+3e^{-x}>0$; division normalizes its trace to one. By [F2] this is a two-qubit density matrix. Its singlet probability is $p_s=e^{3x}/(e^{3x}+3e^{-x})=e^{4x}/(e^{4x}+3)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Using the two eigenvalues in [F1], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xC)=-3p_s+(1-p_s)=1-4p_s=3(1-e^{4x})/(e^{4x}+3)=:c$. For $x\ge0$, $e^{4x}\ge1$, hence $-3\le c\le0$, and $c<-1$ exactly when $e^{4x}>3$, equivalently $x>(\log3)/4$ by [F7]. [given, F1, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $x>(\log3)/4$, step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xC)=c<-1$. This contradicts the lower bound [F5] satisfied by every separable state, so $\rho_x$ is entangled. [given, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 If $0\le x\le(\log3)/4$, step 2.1 gives $-1\le c\le0$. The spectral projections in [F1] give $\rho_x=\tfrac14(I_4+(c/3)C)$; substituting [F6] yields $\rho_x=(-c)\rho_*+(1+c)I_4/4$. Both coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one; [F3] makes $I_2/2$ a qubit density matrix, so $I_4/4=(I_2/2)\otimes(I_2/2)$ is a product density matrix. Thus [F4] and [F6] make $\rho_x$ separable, including at equality $c=-1$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Interacting Heisenberg dimer Gibbs model
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement:
Let $e_0,e_1$ and $\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z,C$ be as in [[def-qsm-pauli-two-qubit-conventions]], with $\sigma_z e_0=e_0$ and $\sigma_z e_1=-e_1$. By [[lem-qsm-pauli-dimer-spectrum]], the normalized singlet $s=(e_0\otimes e_1-e_1\otimes e_0)/\sqrt2$ has $C$-eigenvalue $-3$, and the three orthonormal triplets have eigenvalue $1$. Adopt the two-spin Hamiltonian
$$H_{J,h}:=JC-h(\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z)$$
on $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$, where $J,h\in\mathbb R$ are energies in joules. For inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, use the canonical Gibbs preparation only after normalizing its finite trace. Its singlet energy is $-3J$; its triplet energies are $J-2h$, $J$, and $J+2h$. Here $\cosh y:=(e^y+e^{-y})/2$.
$$Z(\beta,J,h)=e^{3\beta J}+e^{-\beta J}\bigl(1+2\cosh(2\beta h)\bigr)>0.$$
At $h=0$ and $J>0$, the Gibbs density matrix is entangled exactly when $\beta J>(\log3)/4$, and is separable at and below equality. This exact threshold is a finite-state quantum-model conclusion. For every fixed $J,h$, $Z$ and the free energy $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ are real analytic for $\beta>0$; the entanglement threshold is not a finite-temperature thermodynamic singularity. At zero field the entropy tends to $0$ as $\beta\to\infty$ for $J>0$, to $k_B\log3$ for $J<0$, and to $k_B\log4$ for $J=0$. For $J>0$, a nonzero field makes the singlet and the field-aligned triplet cross at $|h|=2J$ at zero temperature; this ground-space crossing does not make $Z$ singular at finite positive temperature.

references.title: Doron Cohen, Lecture Notes in Statistical Mechanics and Mesoscopics, §§2.2–2.3
Damian Markham, Janet Anders, Vlatko Vedral, Mio Murao, and Akimasa Miyake, Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.physical_scope: The finite two-spin Hilbert space C^2 tensor C^2 with the isotropic Pauli exchange Hamiltonian and a uniform z-field, at positive temperature. The exact separability threshold is asserted only at zero field for J>0. There is no measurement, thermalization, material-specific, or infinite-volume claim.
items.strategy:
1.1 In the ordered basis $e_0e_0,e_0e_1,e_1e_0,e_1e_1$, the field operator $\sigma_z\otimes I+I\otimes\sigma_z$ has eigenvalues $2,0,0,-2$. The middle two basis vectors combine into the singlet and the $m=0$ triplet of [F2]; both have field eigenvalue $0$. The outer vectors are the $m=+1$ and $m=-1$ triplets, with field eigenvalues $2$ and $-2$. Since $H_{J,h}$ is a linear combination of these commuting matrices, the singlet energy is $-3J$ and the triplet energies are $J-2h,J,J+2h$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The canonical trace is the sum of the four positive weights associated with step 1.1. It is therefore finite and positive, and the adopted preparation [A1] gives the displayed partition function. At $h=0$ and $J>0$, setting $x=\beta J$ identifies its normalized state with $\rho_x$ in [F3], so that theorem gives the exact separability and entanglement alternatives, including the equality case. [given, A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Fix $J,h$ and let $E_{\min}$ be the least of the four energies from step 1.1, with multiplicity $g$. Write the other energies as $E_{\min}+\Delta_i$ with $\Delta_i>0$. After factoring out $e^{-\beta E_{\min}}$, the denominator is $D_\beta=g+\sum_i e^{-\beta\Delta_i}\to g$ and $1\le D_\beta\le4$. The Gibbs probability of each ground vector is $1/D_\beta$, so the total ground entropy tends to $-k_Bg(1/g)\log(1/g)=k_B\log g$. For an excited vector, $p_i=e^{-\beta\Delta_i}/D_\beta$ and $-p_i\log p_i=p_i(\beta\Delta_i+\log D_\beta)\le e^{-\beta\Delta_i}(\beta\Delta_i+\log4)$; this tends to zero by [F9], so the finite sum of excited entropy terms vanishes. At $h=0$, the triplet is the three-dimensional ground space for $J<0$, all four levels coincide for $J=0$, and the singlet is the unique ground state for $J>0$, giving the stated limits. [A1, F2, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $J,h$ and any $\beta_0>0$. For each of the four energies $E$ from step 1.1, the addition formula [F4] gives $e^{-\beta E}=e^{-\beta_0E}\sum_{n\ge0}[-E(\beta-\beta_0)]^n/n!$, a convergent power series about $\beta_0$. The four-term sum $Z(\beta)$ is therefore real analytic near $\beta_0$ by [F5]–[F6], and $Z(\beta_0)>0$ by step 2.1. Put $y_0=\log Z(\beta_0)$. By [F8], $\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)$; by [F7], $\exp'(y_0)=\exp(y_0)=Z(\beta_0)\ne0$. The real analytic inverse theorem gives a local analytic inverse to $\exp$ near $Z(\beta_0)$, and [F8] identifies that inverse with $\log$. The composition clause of [F6] now makes $\log Z$ real analytic near $\beta_0$. Since $\beta_0$ was arbitrary, $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is real analytic for every $\beta>0$: the identity and constant functions have local polynomial series, so the quotient clause of [F6] makes $\beta\mapsto\beta^{-1}$ analytic on this domain. Thus the finite-volume free energy has no singularity at the entanglement threshold. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 For $J>0$, the lowest triplet energy is $J-2|h|$. It equals the singlet energy $-3J$ exactly at $|h|=2J$. The two energy levels can cross as parameters vary, but step 2.1 is a strictly positive finite sum of exponentials at every $\beta>0$, so this zero-temperature ground-space crossing creates no finite-temperature singularity. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Commuting quantum Ising and nonadditive phase countermodel
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement:
**Periodic commuting Ising model.** For $N\ge2$, let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ and let $Z_i$ act as $\sigma_z$ on tensor factor $i$ and as identity on the others. With periodic indexing $Z_{N+1}=Z_1$, count exactly the $N$ indexed bonds, so $N=2$ has two bonds. For real energies $J,h$ and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt
$$H_N^{\mathrm q}=-J\sum_{i=1}^N Z_iZ_{i+1}-h\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i.$$
In the product eigenbasis $|s_1,\ldots,s_N\rangle$, $s_i\in\{-1,1\}$, its energy equals $H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)=-J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$. Thus the quantum Gibbs density is diagonal in this basis, and its partition function and diagonal probabilities agree exactly with the specified classical finite ring. In particular, when $J\ge0$ and $h=0$, its $\sigma_z$ correlations are those of [[pthm-csm-ising-ring-correlation]]. For all real $J,h$ and $\beta>0$, define $\cosh x:=(e^x+e^{-x})/2$ and $\sinh x:=(e^x-e^{-x})/2$, and put
$$\lambda_\pm=e^{\beta J}\cosh(\beta h)\pm\sqrt{e^{2\beta J}\sinh^2(\beta h)+e^{-2\beta J}}.$$
Then $N^{-1}\log Z_N^{\mathrm q}\to\log\lambda_+$, with every fixed finite order of derivatives converging locally uniformly on compact subsets of $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$. This is the exact commuting one-dimensional model, not a theorem for noncommuting interactions.

**Global three-sector countermodel.** For $N\ge1$ and $\epsilon>0$ joules, let $\mathcal K_N=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C\oplus(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes 2N}$ with its orthogonal direct-sum inner product, and write $I_{4^N}$ for the identity on the final $4^N$-dimensional summand. Let $|A\rangle,|B\rangle$ be the standard unit vectors in the first and second summands, and let $|s\rangle$ range over the standard product basis in the final summand. Define $H_N^{\mathrm g}=0\oplus N\epsilon\oplus2N\epsilon I_{4^N}$, so the basis energies are $E(A)=0$, $E(B)=N\epsilon$, and $E(s)=2N\epsilon$. For $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, define the spectral-shell basis subset $S_{N,\Delta}:=\{v:|E(v)-N\epsilon|\le\Delta\}$ and its uniform state $\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}:=|S_{N,\Delta}|^{-1}\sum_{v\in S_{N,\Delta}}|v\rangle\langle v|$. For $\beta>0$ this finite quantum model has
$$Z_N^{\mathrm g}=1+e^{-\beta N\epsilon}+4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}.$$
For every real $\beta$ as an algebraic finite-weight extension, the normalized exponential-tilt weight of the one-dimensional middle sector is at most $(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$; the shell state above assigns that sector probability $1$. The term “probability” here is the trace of the state against the middle-sector projection $|B\rangle\langle B|$. Also
$$\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}\longrightarrow\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\},\qquad 0\le\frac1N\log Z_N^{\mathrm g}-\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}\le\frac{\log3}{N}.$$
The limiting function has a corner at $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon>0$; the canonical mean energy per member tends to $2\epsilon$ from below, $0$ from above, and $\epsilon$ at $\beta_c$. Every finite-$N$ partition sum is analytic. This global, size-dependent family is not a product of one fixed finite one-site alphabet and makes no claim about local or short-range matter.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, §§5.3.1 and 5.4.2

items.physical_scope: Two explicit finite-dimensional quantum models: a periodic diagonal one-dimensional Ising Hamiltonian and a global N-dependent three-sector Hamiltonian. The first has the exact specified one-dimensional classical correspondence; the second is deliberately non-product-additive. No generic noncommuting lattice theorem or short-range phase claim is asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 Each $Z_i$ is diagonal in the basis $|s_1,\ldots,s_N\rangle$, with eigenvalue $s_i$. Therefore $H_N^{\mathrm q}|s\rangle=H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)|s\rangle$. The finite canonical trace is the sum of these positive weights, so $Z_N^{\mathrm q}=\sum_s e^{-\beta H_N^{\mathrm{cl}}(s)}$ and the diagonal Gibbs probability of each $|s\rangle$ equals the classical probability of $s$. This proves the claimed finite correspondence without interpreting off-diagonal quantum observables classically. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 The direct sum in the second model has multiplicities $1,1,4^N$, so summing its three energy weights gives $Z_N^{\mathrm g}=1+x+4^Nx^2$ where $x=e^{-\beta N\epsilon}>0$. Since $(1-2^Nx)^2\ge0$, $1+4^Nx^2\ge2^{N+1}x$, whence the middle-sector probability $x/Z_N^{\mathrm g}\le(2^{N+1}+1)^{-1}$. For $0\le\Delta<N\epsilon$, the sectors at energies $0$ and $2N\epsilon$ lie exactly $N\epsilon$ from the middle energy; the only basis vector in the shell is $|B\rangle$, so $\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}=|B\rangle\langle B|$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{N,\Delta}^{\mathrm{shell}}|B\rangle\langle B|)=1$. These are the same finite-model values recorded in [F4], now obtained from the explicit Hilbert-space realization. [given, A1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Applying [F2] to this identical finite energy function gives the displayed transfer eigenvalues, limiting normalized log partition, and compact-uniform derivative convergence. Its strict eigenvalue gap and positive $\lambda_+$ imply an analytic finite-temperature limit. In the restricted case $J\ge0,h=0$, the equality of diagonal probabilities from step 1.1 transports each $\sigma_z$ correlation to the classical spin correlation in [F3], under exactly that supplier's hypotheses. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.2 Put $M_N=\max\{1,4^Nx^2\}$. If $x\le1$, then $x\le M_N$; if $x>1$, then $4^Nx^2\ge x$ for $N\ge1$. Hence $M_N\le Z_N^{\mathrm g}\le3M_N$, and $N^{-1}\log M_N=\max\{0,\log4-2\beta\epsilon\}$. Taking logarithms gives the stated error bound and limit. Since $\log4=2\log2$, the two branches meet at $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon$. For $\beta<\beta_c$, the $4^Nx^2$ sector dominates and the mean energy per member tends to $2\epsilon$; for $\beta>\beta_c>0$, the energy-zero sector dominates and the mean tends to $0$. At equality the three weights are $1,2^{-N},1$, so the mean tends to $\epsilon$. [given, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Each finite partition function in both models is a finite sum of positive real exponentials, so it is real analytic and has no finite-$N$ thermodynamic singularity. The Ising limiting analytic statement follows under [F2]'s positive eigenvalue gap; the corner in step 2.2 belongs only to the separate non-product-additive limiting family. [given, F2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact onsite Bose and Fermi interacting atoms
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement:
**Repulsive single-mode Bose site.** Let $\mathcal H_B=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n\rangle$, supplied by the one-mode specialization of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]]. Put $E_B(n):=\epsilon n+\frac U2n(n-1)$, where $\epsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $U>0$ are in joules. Define $H_B$ and $N_B$ as real diagonal multipliers $H_B|n\rangle=E_B(n)|n\rangle$ and $N_B|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$ on their maximal domains
$$D(H_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}E_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(N_B)=\left\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, define $K_B$ directly as the real diagonal multiplier with eigenvalues
$$K_B(n):=E_B(n)-\mu n=\frac U2n^2+\left(\epsilon-\mu-\frac U2\right)n$$
on the exact maximal domain $D(K_B)=\{c\in\ell^2:\sum_{n\ge0}K_B(n)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. These diagonal multipliers are self-adjoint on their displayed domains. The grand partition sum
$$\Xi_B(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$$
is finite and positive for every such $(\beta,\mu)$. It is jointly real analytic locally on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, meaning it has an absolutely convergent power-series representation in the two real parameters near every point. Its normalized diagonal Gibbs state has weights $p_n=\Xi_B^{-1}e^{-\beta K_B(n)}$ and
$$\langle N_B\rangle=\Xi_B^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}n e^{-\beta K_B(n)},\qquad \partial_\mu\langle N_B\rangle=\beta\,\operatorname{Var}(N_B).$$
In the zero-temperature limit $\beta\to\infty$, the unique minimizing occupation is $0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, and is $r\ge1$ when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$. At each boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$, exactly the adjacent occupations $r,r+1$ minimize $K_B$; their probabilities tend to $1/2$ each and the model entropy $S=-k_B\operatorname{tr}(\rho_B\log\rho_B)$ from [[post-qsm-models-statistics-and-preparation]] tends to $k_B\log2$. In a strict interval, the unique minimizing number state has probability tending to one and entropy tending to zero.

**Two-mode Fermi Hubbard atom.** On $\mathcal H_F=\mathbb C^4$ with orthonormal occupation basis $|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, $n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\in\{0,1\}$, define $n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\uparrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$ and $n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle=n_\downarrow|n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow\rangle$, and adopt
$$H_F=\epsilon(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)+U n_\uparrow n_\downarrow-h(n_\uparrow-n_\downarrow),$$
where $\epsilon,\mu,U,h$ are in joules, $U\ge0$, and $\beta>0$. With $K_F=H_F-\mu(n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow)$, its grand partition function and weights are
$$\Xi_F=1+w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+w_2,\quad w_\uparrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu-h)},\quad w_\downarrow=e^{-\beta(\epsilon-\mu+h)},\quad w_2=e^{-\beta(2(\epsilon-\mu)+U)}.$$
Thus $\langle n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_\downarrow+2w_2)/\Xi_F$, the double-occupation probability $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle$ is $w_2/\Xi_F$, and, with $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow):=\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle-\langle n_\uparrow\rangle\langle n_\downarrow\rangle$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=\frac{e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}(e^{-\beta U}-1)}{\Xi_F^2}\le0.$$
The covariance is zero at $U=0$ and strictly negative at $U>0$. These are exact conditional model calculations, not claims about measured atoms.

references.title: Immanuel Bloch, Jean Dalibard, and Wilhelm Zwerger, Many-body physics with ultracold gases, §§IV.A and IV.E
David Tong, Statistical Physics, §§3.5–3.6

items.physical_scope: One isolated single-mode repulsive Bose site and one isolated two-spin-mode Fermi Hubbard atom in finite-temperature grand-canonical model states. The Bose interaction U is strictly positive; the Fermi interaction is nonnegative. No hopping, lattice thermodynamic limit, material-specific prediction, or empirical observation is asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 The one-mode case of [F1] identifies the number basis with the standard basis of $\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$, whose finite-support span is dense. For any real diagonal multiplier with entries $\lambda_n$, testing the adjoint identity on each basis vector forces the adjoint image to have coordinates $\lambda_nc_n$, so its adjoint domain is contained in $\{c:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\}$. Conversely, on that weighted domain [F11] makes the pairing bounded and identifies the adjoint action with the same multiplier. Thus its maximal diagonal domain is self-adjoint. Applying this calculation to $E_B(n)$, $n$, and $K_B(n)$ establishes the three domains in the Statement. [given, F1, F2, F11, algebra]

1.2 Consecutive Bose grand energies on the number basis [F1] satisfy $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=\epsilon-\mu+Un$, a strictly increasing affine sequence in $n$. It is positive at every $n\ge0$ when $\mu<\epsilon$, so $0$ uniquely minimizes. For $r\ge1$, it is negative through $n=r-1$ and positive from $n=r$ exactly when $\epsilon+U(r-1)<\mu<\epsilon+Ur$, so $r$ uniquely minimizes. At $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increment at $n=r$ is zero while all earlier increments are negative and all later increments positive; exactly $r,r+1$ minimize. [given, F1, algebra]

1.3 The four Fermi basis states have grand energies $0$, $\epsilon-\mu-h$, $\epsilon-\mu+h$, and $2(\epsilon-\mu)+U$, respectively. Summing their four positive weights gives the displayed $\Xi_F$, and summing $n_\uparrow+n_\downarrow$ or $n_\uparrow n_\downarrow$ against those weights gives the stated mean and double-occupation probability. The state is well-defined because this is a finite positive sum, as required by [A1] and [F3]. [given, A1, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Put $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$. Completing the square gives $K_B(n)=\frac U4n^2+\frac U4(n+2a/U)^2-a^2/U\ge\frac U4n^2-a^2/U$. For $n\ge1$, $n^2\ge n$, so $e^{-\beta K_B(n)}\le e^{\beta a^2/U}q^n$ with $q=e^{-\beta U/4}$. Since $\beta U/4>0$, [F5] gives $0<q<1$, and [F6] makes the geometric upper bound summable. The $n=0$ term is $1$, so $0<\Xi_B<\infty$ and [A1], [F3] give a well-defined normalized grand state. The free-mode product trace formula in [F2] is not used. [given, A1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 In a strict interval with unique minimizer $r$, let $\delta$ be the smaller positive adjacent energy gap from $r$ (use only the upward gap when $r=0$). For $n>r$, the gap is a sum of increments from step 1.2, each at least the upward gap at $r$; for $n<r$, it is a sum of reversed increments, each at least the downward gap from $r-1$. Hence $K_B(n)-K_B(r)\ge\delta|n-r|$. The total relative excited weight is therefore at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=2e^{-\beta\delta}/(1-e^{-\beta\delta})$, which tends to zero. At a boundary $\mu=\epsilon+Ur$, the increments are $K_B(n+1)-K_B(n)=U(n-r)$, so exactly $r,r+1$ minimize. To the right, $K_B(r+1+\ell)-K_B(r+1)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$; to the left, $K_B(r-\ell)-K_B(r)=U(1+\cdots+\ell)\ge U\ell$ whenever $r\ge\ell$. Thus the total relative excited weight is at most $2\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta U\ell}=2e^{-\beta U}/(1-e^{-\beta U})$. The normalized Gibbs probabilities from [F3] therefore concentrate on the unique number state in a strict interval, or tend to $1/2,1/2$ on the adjacent pair at a boundary. [given, F3, step 1.2, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 Fix $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ with $\beta_0>0$, put $u=\beta-\beta_0$, $v=\mu-\mu_0$, $a_0=\epsilon-\mu_0-U/2$, and $K_n^0=Un^2/2+a_0n$. Then $-\beta K_B(n;\mu)=-\beta_0K_n^0-uK_n^0+\beta_0vn+uvn$, so [F5] expands each summand as $e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}e^{-uK_n^0}e^{\beta_0vn}e^{uvn}$. On radii $r_\beta=\beta_0/2$ and any fixed $r_\mu>0$, the sum of the absolute values of all terms of these three exponential power series, over all $n$, is bounded by $\sum_{n\ge0}\exp(-\beta_0K_n^0+r_\beta|K_n^0|+\beta_0r_\mu n+r_\beta r_\mu n)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $K_n^0\ge0$ and $|K_n^0|\le Un^2/2+|a_0|n$, so the exponent is at most $-\beta_0Un^2/4+Cn$ for a finite constant $C$. Increasing the cutoff so $Cn\le\beta_0Un^2/8$ leaves a tail bounded by $e^{-\beta_0Un/8}$, whose series converges by [F5]–[F6]; the finitely many initial terms are finite. Thus the total absolute coefficient sum is finite. Grouping $r+t=p$ and $s+t=q$ gives $c_{pq}=\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-\beta_0K_n^0}\sum_{t=0}^{\min(p,q)}\frac{(-K_n^0)^{p-t}(\beta_0n)^{q-t}n^t}{(p-t)!(q-t)!t!}$. The absolute bound and [F7] justify these coefficient sums and rearrangement, and give $\sum_{p,q}|c_{pq}|r_\beta^p r_\mu^q<\infty$, hence $|c_{pq}|\le M r_\beta^{-p}r_\mu^{-q}$ for some finite $M$. Applying the multivariable power-series theorem [F7] gives a holomorphic sum on the complex polydisc; its real restriction is the absolutely convergent germ in [F4]. Since $(\beta_0,\mu_0)$ was arbitrary, $\Xi_B$ is jointly real analytic on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. [given, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Fix $\beta>0$ and let $\mu$ range over a compact interval. The quantity $a=\epsilon-\mu-U/2$ is then bounded, so the square bound in step 2.1 gives $e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C e^{-\beta U n^2/4}$ for a constant $C$ uniform on that interval. Put $q=e^{-\beta U/8}\in(0,1)$. Since $n^2\ge n$, $(1+n^2)e^{-\beta K_B(n;\mu)}\le C(1+n^2)q^{2n}$. By [F9], $(1+n^2)q^n$ is bounded, so the right side is at most $C'q^n$, a summable geometric envelope. Apply [F8] on $\mathbb N_0$ with the counting measure [A2], weight $w(n)=e^{-\beta E_B(n)}$, observable $X(n)=n$, and natural parameter $\theta=\beta\mu$. Its hypotheses hold by this compact envelope and step 2.1; it gives $\partial_\theta\mathbb E(N_B)=\operatorname{Var}(N_B)$. The chain rule [F12] yields the displayed response, while the normalized weights give the expectation formula. [given, A2, F3, F5, F6, F8, F9, F12, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 Let $g=1$ in a strict interval and $g=2$ at a boundary, and shift all energies by their minimum so the ground energy is zero. The diagonal entropy from [F3] is $S_B/k_B=\log D_\beta+\beta\sum_{n\ge0}p_nK_B(n)$, where $D_\beta=g+R_\beta$ and $R_\beta$ is the total relative excited weight from step 2.2. Thus $D_\beta\to g$ by step 2.2 and $\log D_\beta\to\log g$ by continuity [F10]. In either case, for each distance $\ell\ge1$ there are at most two excited states; their lower gaps are $\delta\ell$ by step 2.2 and their upper gaps are $C(1+\ell^2)$ because $K_B(n)$ is quadratic in $n$. Here $C$ is fixed and $\delta=U$ at a boundary. For $\beta\ge1$, [F9] makes $(1+\ell^2)e^{-\delta\ell/2}$ bounded; splitting $e^{-\beta\delta\ell}=e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}$ therefore bounds $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}(1+\ell^2)e^{-\beta\delta\ell}$ by a constant times $\beta\sum_{\ell\ge1}e^{-\beta\delta\ell/2}=\beta q_\beta/(1-q_\beta)$, where $q_\beta=e^{-\beta\delta/2}$. This tends to zero by [F5], [F6], and [F9]. Consequently the excited contribution to the entropy vanishes, while the normalized ground weights contribute $0$ for $g=1$ and $\log2$ for $g=2$. [given, F3, F5, F6, F9, F10, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The normalized means are $\langle n_\uparrow\rangle=(w_\uparrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$ and $\langle n_\downarrow\rangle=(w_\downarrow+w_2)/\Xi_F$, while $\langle n_\uparrow n_\downarrow\rangle=w_2/\Xi_F$. Subtracting the product of the means yields $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=(w_2-w_\uparrow w_\downarrow)/\Xi_F^2$. Since $w_\uparrow w_\downarrow=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}$ and $w_2=e^{-2\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}e^{-\beta U}$, this is the displayed formula; $U\ge0$ makes it nonpositive, with equality exactly at $U=0$. [given, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

title: Finite Pauli dimer spectrum and exact separability threshold — Examples

items.title: Finite analyticity versus the global-model cusp and shell inequivalence
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement: For the global three-sector model of [[pthm-qsm-commuting-lattice-countermodels]], take $N=2$ and $\beta_c=(\log2)/\epsilon$. Its finite Gibbs probability of the one-dimensional middle sector is exactly $1/9$, while a uniform spectral shell with half-width $0\le\Delta<2\epsilon$ assigns that sector probability $1$. The finite partition function is still analytic at $\beta_c$; the cusp belongs to the limiting normalized log partition as $N\to\infty$.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, §§5.3.1 and 5.4.2

items.physical_scope: The N=2 member and positive transition parameter of the explicitly defined finite global three-sector quantum model. This is not an example of a local or short-range quantum lattice.
items.strategy:
1.1 At $N=2$ and $\beta=\beta_c$, $e^{-\beta N\epsilon}=e^{-2\log2}=1/4$ and $4^Ne^{-2\beta N\epsilon}=16e^{-4\log2}=1$. Hence $Z_2=9/4$ and the middle-sector Gibbs probability is $(1/4)/(9/4)=1/9$. The finite partition is a sum of positive exponentials, so it is analytic at this parameter. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $2\epsilon$ is the distance from the middle energy to either outer energy at $N=2$, every shell with $0\le\Delta<2\epsilon$ selects exactly the one-dimensional middle sector and gives it uniform probability $1$. Thus the two specified finite preparations disagree on this observable, while the analytic finite sum and limiting cusp remain distinct claims. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Entanglement threshold versus thermodynamic singularity
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement: For the zero-field dimer of [[pthm-qsm-interacting-dimer-gibbs]] with $J>0$, the equality point $\beta J=(\log3)/4$ gives a separable Gibbs density matrix, and every larger $\beta J$ gives an entangled one. Nevertheless $Z=e^{3\beta J}+3e^{-\beta J}$ and the free energy remain analytic at this threshold. The threshold changes the separability classification without producing a finite-temperature thermodynamic singularity.

references.title: Damian Markham, Janet Anders, Vlatko Vedral, Mio Murao, and Akimasa Miyake, Survival of entanglement in thermal states, Example 1

items.physical_scope: The zero-field, antiferromagnetic finite Pauli dimer at its exact thermal separability boundary. It distinguishes a state-property threshold from a thermodynamic singularity and makes no experimental claim.
items.strategy:
1.1 Substituting $\beta J=(\log3)/4$ into [F1] gives the separable equality state; taking any $\beta J>(\log3)/4$ gives the entangled branch. These are conclusions about the defined two-qubit density matrix. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At $h=0$, $Z=e^{3\beta J}+3e^{-\beta J}$ is a finite positive sum of exponentials, so $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$ is analytic for $\beta>0$, including at the separability threshold. Therefore this state-property boundary is not a thermodynamic singularity of the finite dimer. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Repulsive Fermi covariance and zero-temperature Bose occupation step
items.design_state: Reserved by the complete assigned design section; authored as a draft in batch 46.
items.statement: For the Fermi atom of [[pthm-qsm-onsite-interacting-atoms]], set $h=0$, $\mu=\epsilon$, and $U>0$. Then $\Xi_F=3+e^{-\beta U}$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(n_\uparrow,n_\downarrow)=(e^{-\beta U}-1)/(3+e^{-\beta U})^2<0$. For the Bose site, set $\mu=\epsilon+U$ with $U>0$; the two zero-temperature minimizing occupations are $1$ and $2$, each with limiting Gibbs probability $1/2$, and the entropy tends to $k_B\log2$.

references.title: Immanuel Bloch, Jean Dalibard, and Wilhelm Zwerger, Many-body physics with ultracold gases, §§IV.A and IV.E

items.physical_scope: A symmetric-parameter instance of the finite Fermi atom and a single Bose zero-temperature boundary in the isolated onsite models. No lattice or material-specific conclusion is drawn.
items.strategy:
1.1 Substituting $h=0$ and $\mu=\epsilon$ into the Fermi weights gives $w_\uparrow=w_\downarrow=1$, $w_2=e^{-\beta U}$, and $\Xi_F=3+e^{-\beta U}$. Since $U,\beta>0$, $e^{-\beta U}<1$, so [F1] gives the strictly negative covariance stated in the Example. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 In the Bose result of [F1], set $r=1$ and $\mu=\epsilon+U$. The adjacent minimizing occupations are $1,2$, their limiting probabilities are $1/2,1/2$, and the binary entropy is $-k_B(2)(1/2)\log(1/2)=k_B\log2$. [given, F1, algebra] ∎
